# Eugenics, Jordan, and the Science of Social Control {#sec-3-03}

::: {.chapter-meta}
Act III — Hoover, War, and the Archive State · 1900–1913
:::

::: {.content-visible when-profile="draft"}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Pre-Draft Brief

**Core question.** How does an institution justify inequality?

**The answer.** It calls the inequality natural. Stanford's first president was
a biologist and one of the most prominent American eugenicists of his
generation, and California became the most aggressive sterilising jurisdiction
in the United States under a law passed in 1909. The university did not merely
educate the people who would lead. It supplied the scientific argument for why
they should.

**The mechanism.** Elite network reproduction, with the ideology made explicit.
This is the chapter where the legitimacy layer stops being implicit: an
institution built on monopoly rent produces a science of who is fit, and the
science ranks the institution's own constituency at the top. The book's most
serious charge, and it requires the most careful sourcing.

**The key fact.** California's 1909 sterilisation law made the state responsible
for roughly a third of all recorded sterilisations in the United States. Cite a
range with its basis rather than a single round figure — institutional records
and retrospective studies do not agree, and the disagreement is part of the
story.

**The human anchor.** David Starr Jordan: ichthyologist, university president,
conservationist, peace campaigner, and eugenicist — all genuinely, all at once.
Do not simplify him. The chapter is more damning if he is a whole person.

**Excluded voices.** The people sterilised, overwhelmingly poor,
disproportionately Mexican and Black, institutionalised and unable to consent.
They are the chapter's actual subject and they must be present as people, using
what the record preserves.

**Proof.** This chapter proves that the institution produced a justification for
hierarchy alongside the hierarchy by showing its founding president advancing a
biological argument for social sorting while the state enacted it in law.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Working summary

California's 1909 sterilisation law is written in flat administrative prose, and
the chapter opens by quoting it. Under that statute and its successors the state
performed roughly a third of all recorded sterilisations in the United States.
The figures vary between institutional records and later studies, and the
chapter cites a range with its basis rather than a round number, because the
disagreement about how many is part of what the record does to people.

David Starr Jordan is presented whole. He was a serious ichthyologist,
Stanford's first president, a conservationist with Sierra Club connections, a
committed peace campaigner, and one of the most prominent eugenicists in America
— all of it genuinely, and all of it in the same paragraph rather than in
separate ones. The chapter is more damning for refusing to simplify him.

The intellectual structure is what matters. Eugenics made heredity explain
poverty, which meant that social hierarchy could be described as biological
rather than economic. For an institution whose endowment came from monopoly
rent, that is an extraordinarily useful proposition: it explains the
distribution of wealth as a distribution of fitness. The university did not
merely educate the people who would lead. It supplied the scientific argument
for why they should, and this is the most serious charge the book makes.

The chapter traces the connection between conservation, national vigour, and
racial exclusion carefully, because it is real and it is frequently overstated.
It notes Berkeley's parallel track in urban planning and restrictive covenants —
the science of sorting applied to a map. And it makes one verified forward
reference, no more, to what lies outside its window: the Human Betterment
Foundation in 1928, and German officials studying California's programme in the
following decade.

The longest section belongs to the people sterilised — overwhelmingly poor,
disproportionately Mexican and Black, institutionalised at Sonoma and Patton,
unable to consent. They are the chapter's subject, and the record preserves
enough to write them as people.

When Act IV calls this talent identification, the reader should hear this
chapter underneath it.
:::

## Beats

1. **Hook.** The 1909 statute, quoted. Legislative prose describing what it
   authorises, in its own flat language.
2. **Jordan whole.** Fish taxonomy, the presidency, the Sierra Club connection,
   the peace advocacy. Then the eugenics, in the same paragraph, not a later
   one.
3. **The argument's structure.** How heredity was made to explain poverty, and
   why that was attractive to an institution whose endowment came from monopoly.
4. **Conservation and national vigour.** The link between wilderness
   preservation, racial anxiety, and fitness. Handle precisely; it is real and
   it is frequently overstated.
5. **The 1909 law.** What it authorised, who administered it, and where. Sonoma
   and Patton by name.
6. **The numbers.** A sourced range with its basis. Explain why the figures
   differ; the methodology is not a distraction from the horror, it is part of
   it.
7. **The people.** Individual cases from the record. This beat is the chapter,
   and it should be the longest.
8. **The export, flagged forward.** German officials studied California's
   programme in the 1920s and 1930s, and the Human Betterment Foundation was
   founded in 1928 — both outside this chapter's window. One forward-pointing
   sentence, verified, and no more.
9. **Berkeley's parallel.** Urban planning, restrictive covenants, and the
   beginnings of redlining. The science of sorting applied to a map.
10. **Landing.** The management science is a sorting science. When Act IV calls
   it talent identification, the reader should hear this chapter under it.
:::

:::

::: {.chapter-question}
How does an institution justify inequality?
:::

The California statute of 1909 is written in the flat administrative prose of a
public health measure. It authorised the medical superintendents of state
institutions to perform an operation on inmates when, in their judgment, it
would improve the person's physical, mental, or moral condition. It required no
consent from the patient. It required no court order.

Over the following decades California sterilised more people under this
authority than any other state in the union — by most reconstructions, something
in the region of a third of the national total. Figures vary between
institutional records and later studies, and the variation is itself part of the
record: the people this was done to were not, in general, considered worth
counting carefully.

This chapter is about where the argument for it came from, and the answer
involves the president of the university this book is about.

## Jordan whole

David Starr Jordan was one of the most distinguished American scientists of his
generation. He was an ichthyologist of the first rank who described a very large
number of fish species and whose taxonomic work is still cited. He was president
of Indiana University at thirty-four and Stanford's first president at thirty-
nine. He was a serious conservationist with connections to the Sierra Club. He
was, notably and at some cost to himself, a committed pacifist who campaigned
against American entry into the First World War.

He was also chairman of the eugenics committee of the American Breeders
Association, an early and influential advocate of sterilisation legislation, and
the author of works arguing that the quality of a nation is a matter of heredity
and that social policy should be organised accordingly.

All of this is the same man, at the same time, and the chapter is more damning
for refusing to separate the parts. Eugenics in the first decades of the
twentieth century was not a fringe enthusiasm held by cranks. It was mainstream
progressive science, held by university presidents, public health officials,
conservationists, and social reformers, and it was attractive precisely to
people who believed that expertise should govern.

## What the argument actually claimed

The structure of the eugenic argument matters more than its scientific content,
which was wrong.

It held that socially significant human characteristics — intelligence,
criminality, pauperism, alcoholism, what was then called feeblemindedness — were
substantially hereditary. From that premise several conclusions followed. Social
problems were biological rather than economic. Charity that allowed the unfit to
reproduce made things worse. And the state had a legitimate interest in who
reproduced.

Now consider what that proposition does for an institution whose endowment came
from a railroad monopoly.

It explains the distribution of wealth as a distribution of quality. If ability
is hereditary and success tracks ability, then a class that has accumulated
enormous advantages has done so because it is better, and its children will
inherit both the money and the merit that justifies it. The argument converts a
structural outcome into a natural one, which is the most useful thing any
ideology can do for the people at the top of a hierarchy.

The university did not merely educate the people who would run California. It
supplied the scientific account of why they should. That is the most serious
charge in this book, and it is made on the basis of the participants' own
published work.

## Conservation and vigour

The link between conservation, national fitness, and racial anxiety is real, and
it is frequently overstated, so the chapter states it precisely.

A strand of early twentieth-century American conservation was explicitly
concerned with the physical and racial quality of the population. Wilderness was
valued partly as a corrective to the supposed degeneration produced by urban
industrial life, and several prominent conservationists were also prominent
eugenicists. Madison Grant, a founder of major conservation organisations, wrote
one of the most influential racist tracts of the period.

This does not mean conservation was a eugenic project, and the chapter does not
say so. It means the two movements drew on an overlapping constituency and an
overlapping vocabulary about national vigour, and that some of the same people
were in both.

## What was done, and to whom

The 1909 law was amended and broadened in 1913 and again in 1917. The operations
were performed in state institutions — the Sonoma State Home, Patton State
Hospital, Stockton, and others — on people committed to them.

The population sterilised was overwhelmingly poor. It included people committed
for mental illness, for intellectual disability as then assessed, and in a
substantial number of cases for behaviour: young women committed as sexually
delinquent, people committed for petty criminality, and children committed
because their families could not keep them.

It was racially disproportionate. Later analyses of the institutional records
have found that Mexican-American and Black patients were sterilised at rates
significantly above their share of the institutional population, and that the
assessments justifying the procedures relied on intelligence testing
administered in English to people who did not speak it.

Consent, where recorded at all, was frequently obtained from a relative or was a
condition of release. A person could be told that the operation was the route
out of the institution.

The record preserves individual cases in enough detail to write them as people,
and the chapter should do so, because the aggregate figure is the least
informative thing about this.

## Beyond the window

Two developments fall outside this chapter's period and warrant one verified
sentence each, because leaving them out would misrepresent the trajectory.

The Human Betterment Foundation was established in Pasadena in 1928 by E. S.
Gosney, with Jordan among the figures associated with the eugenics movement in
California, and it promoted the state's sterilisation programme through
published studies distributed internationally.

And German officials and scientists studied California's programme in the 1920s
and 1930s, and California's example was cited in the German debate that preceded
the 1933 sterilisation law. The direction of influence in this period runs from
California to Germany.

## The map

The same decades produced a parallel application of the sorting principle, and
it was applied to land rather than to bodies.

Restrictive covenants — clauses written into property deeds prohibiting sale or
occupancy by specified racial and religious groups — spread widely across
California in this period and became standard in new subdivisions. They were
private agreements between property owners, enforceable in court, and they did
not require any legislature to pass anything. The Supreme Court held them
judicially unenforceable only in 1948, and their language stayed in deeds for
decades afterwards.

The federal government then systematised the logic. From the mid-1930s the Home
Owners' Loan Corporation and the Federal Housing Administration produced
residential security maps grading neighbourhoods for lending risk, with the
lowest grade marked in red. Racial and ethnic composition was an explicit factor
in the grading, and the underwriting manuals of the period recommended
restrictive covenants as a means of maintaining neighbourhood stability.

The consequence is that the geography of the Bay Area — who could buy where, who
could accumulate housing equity, and whose neighbourhoods received investment —
was determined by documents that ranked populations by supposed quality. When
Act IV describes the Stanford Research Park and asks who could live within reach
of the jobs, this is the answer, and it was drawn on a map.

The same intellectual move underlies both. A class of experts identifies human
quality, ranks it, and acts on the ranking, and the ranking is recorded in an
instrument — a commitment order, a deed, an underwriting map — that outlasts the
belief that produced it.

## The sorting science

California's sterilisation laws remained on the books until 1979. Coerced
sterilisations in California institutions and prisons have been documented well
beyond that date, including cases in state prisons in the first decade of this
century, and the state established a compensation programme for survivors in
2021.

What Act III will call the science of management is, in this chapter, visibly
the science of sorting: the claim that a class of experts can identify human
quality, rank it, and act on the ranking, for the good of everyone.

The claim will change vocabulary repeatedly over the next century. It becomes
scientific management, then aptitude testing, then admissions, then talent
identification, then pattern recognition about founders. When Act IV describes a
venture capitalist explaining that he can tell within twenty minutes whether
someone will succeed, the reader should hear this chapter underneath it.
